summary: Defines an option for negotiating header compression on IP datagrams over the Point-to-Point Protocol, by extending the PPP control protocols for IPv4 and IPv6. Compression can apply to IP headers combined with TCP, UDP, and RTP. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Each message carries a long label that is often the same. This memo lets the two ends of a link agree to use a short nickname for the label to save space.

questions: what is ip header compression over ppp
what is the ppp ip-compression-protocol option
how does ppp negotiate header compression
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree to shrink IP, TCP, UDP and RTP headers.

tldr.problem: Packet headers are bulky and often repeat from packet to packet. Before a PPP link can use header compression, both ends must agree on its parameters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3544 defines an IP-Compression-Protocol option for the IPv4 and IPv6 PPP control protocols (IPCP and IPV6CP). It carries the context limits and timers, plus suboptions for RTP and for TCP-only or non-TCP-only compression. It also defines nine PPP protocol field values that label the compressed frame types.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3544 obsoletes RFC 2509 and adds two suboptions. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3544 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2509, adding the two new suboptions.

sections.title: Why Negotiate Header Compression
sections.content:
The IP Header Compression scheme (IPHC) in RFC 2507 can compress both IPv4 and IPv6 headers, and TCP and UDP headers too. The IP/UDP/RTP compression in RFC 2508 and RFC 3545 fits inside the same framework.

To use compression on a PPP link, each end must agree on a set of configuration parameters. PPP negotiates network layer settings with network control protocols (NCPs). Since IPv4 and IPv6 have separate NCPs, this document defines a configuration option that works in both.

IPHC uses delta encoding for TCP and RTP, which normally needs a link that does not reorder packets. PPP does not reorder packets, so the reordering mechanisms from RFC 2507 are disabled by default. With multiclass multilink PPP, packets that share a compression context must not be reordered.
sections.eli5: Before two friends start using secret nicknames, they have to agree on the rules. This memo is how two computers on a phone-style line agree on the nickname rules.

sections.title: The Configuration Option
sections.content:
The option reuses the IPCP IP-Compression-Protocol option from RFC 1332, with the compression protocol value 0061 (hex). The same format is used in IPCP and in IPV6CP (RFC 2472). The option has Type 2 and a Length of at least 14. The length grows if suboptions are added.

The option describes the capabilities of the decompressor, the receiving side, of the peer that sends the Config-Req. Successful negotiation enables the protocol identifiers FULL_HEADER, COMPRESSED_TCP, COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA, COMPRESSED_NON_TCP and CONTEXT_STATE.

  • TCP_SPACE: the highest context identifier for TCP, from 0 to 255. Suggested value 15. A value of 0 still means one context.
  • NON_TCP_SPACE: the highest context identifier for non-TCP, from 0 to 65535. Suggested value 15.
  • F_MAX_PERIOD: no more than this many COMPRESSED_NON_TCP headers between full headers. Suggested value 256. Zero means no limit.
  • F_MAX_TIME: the longest time in seconds after a FULL_HEADER before COMPRESSED_NON_TCP headers must stop. Suggested value 5. Zero means infinity.
  • MAX_HEADER: the largest header size in octets that may be compressed. Suggested value 168. It should be large enough to compress at least the outer network layer header.

Multiple instances of the IP-Compression-Protocol option are allowed, each with a different compression protocol value, as RFC 3241 clarifies. Each compression protocol sets its own parameters.
sections.eli5: The option is a form with boxes: how many nicknames you can keep, how often to send the full label again, and how long a label you will shrink. Each end fills it in.

sections.title: Suboptions
sections.content:
After the fixed fields, the option may carry zero or more suboptions. Each has a type, a length covering the whole suboption including the type and length fields, and parameter octets.

  • Suboption 1, RTP-Compression (length 2): include it to enable IP/UDP/RTP compression. It enables COMPRESSED_RTP, COMPRESSED_UDP and CONTEXT_STATE as in RFC 2508.
  • Suboption 2, Enhanced RTP-Compression (length 2): enables the RFC 3545 form of compression. It is negotiated instead of, not in addition to, suboption 1.
  • Suboption 3, TCP-only or non-TCP-only (length 3): one parameter byte. A value of 1 means the number of TCP contexts is 0. A value of 2 means the number of non-TCP contexts is 0.

Suboption 3 exists because under RFC 2509 a value of 0 in TCP_SPACE or NON_TCP_SPACE still meant one context, so one kind of compression could not be turned off. Suboption 3 overrides the earlier TCP_SPACE and NON_TCP_SPACE values. If it appears with both parameters 1 and 2, compression is disabled for all packets.
sections.eli5: Suboptions are extra stickers on the form. One says "also shrink phone-call packets", and one says "only shrink this kind, not that kind".

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Together
sections.content:
IPHC compresses both IPv6 and IPv4 datagrams, and both IPCP and IPV6CP can negotiate its parameters. The values from IPCP apply to packets whose outer header is IPv4, and those from IPV6CP apply where the outer header is IPv6.

The context identifier space is shared between IPv4 and IPv6 headers, even when the negotiated values differ. The compressor must allocate identifiers from a common pool, and for compressed packets the decompressor looks at the context state to learn which parameters to use. The space is not shared between TCP and non-TCP/UDP/RTP, because switching an identifier from one to the other would need extra mechanisms to prevent errors.
sections.eli5: Both kinds of addresses share one set of nicknames, like two classes sharing one coat rack. TCP and the others each get their own rack, so coats never get mixed up.

sections.title: Labelling Compressed Frames
sections.content:
The link layer must tell the receiver which header format a frame holds. RFC 2507 defines four compressed formats plus the full header, and RFC 2508 adds compressed UDP and RTP with 8- or 16-bit context identifiers, plus an explicit error message from the decompressor. This document specifies nine values for the PPP Data Link Layer Protocol field, one for each.

The two non-TCP formats from RFC 2507 can be told apart by their contents, so both share the COMPRESSED_NON_TCP value. A full header differs from a regular header because it carries extra information to set up shared context between compressor and decompressor.
sections.eli5: Each frame gets a coloured tag so the receiver knows which kind of shrunk label it holds and how to unshrink it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Negotiating this option adds no security concerns beyond those of PPP itself. The RFC notes that header compression can, in rare cases, cause packets to be delivered to the wrong place. If packet contents must be confidential, they should be encrypted.

Encryption at the IP layer, such as IPsec, prevents compression of the encrypted headers, although the outer IP header and the authentication and security headers can still be compressed. For RTP, full header compression is possible if only the RTP payload is encrypted and the UDP and RTP headers are left clear, which suits cases where that header information need not be confidential.
sections.eli5: Shrinking labels can very rarely send a letter to the wrong house. If a letter is secret, lock it in an envelope. A locked envelope's label cannot be shrunk.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document needs no new allocations in the IANA PPP field assignments registry. It does record that three namespaces defined by RFC 1332, RFC 2472 and RFC 2509 were added to the registry: the IP-Compression-Protocol types, the IPv6-Compression-Protocol types, and the IP Header Compression Configuration Option Suboption Types.

This document defines two new suboption types beyond the one in RFC 2509. Because few more are expected, anyone who wants to define a new suboption must produce a revision of this document through the normal Internet Standards process. The nine protocol field values repeat RFC 2509 without change.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the numbers used, and this memo adds two new entries to the list of stickers. Anyone wanting more stickers has to update this memo.

fields.name: MAX_HEADER
fields.desc: Largest header size that may be compressed.

items.label: FULL_HEADER
items.desc: Full header that sets up shared context.

items.label: COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA
items.desc: Compressed TCP header without delta encoding.
